item.title: One of Russia's most active volcanoes rises above a sea of clouds - AOL.com
item.summary: Volcanic activity at Shivelyuch had persisted for several months when Landsat 9 acquired this image. Watching volcanoes from space. Monitoring a ...
item.page_text:
Today’s Image of the Day features one of Russia’s most active volcanoes rising above a blanket of clouds on the Kamchatka Peninsula.
Snow covers the upper slopes of Shivelyuch, while a dark formation near the summit offers a glimpse of the volcanic activity taking place within the mountain.
The image was captured on November 8, 2026, by the Operational Land Imager aboard Landsat 9 . Although clouds concealed much of the surrounding landscape, the volcano’s summit remained visible from space.
The contrast between the snowy mountainside and the exposed volcanic rock offers a striking portrait of a landscape that is continually being rebuilt from within.
Shivelyuch, also known as Shiveluch, is among the largest and most active volcanoes on the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia’s Far East.
The mountain has a complex geological history. Its older structure, known as Stary Shiveluch, dates back roughly 65,000 years.
A younger volcanic complex, Molodoy Shiveluch, subsequently developed within the remains of the older mountain.
The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program has documented at least 60 major eruptions at Shivelyuch during the Holocene, the geological epoch that began approximately 11,700 years ago.
Successive eruptions and collapses have left extensive deposits of volcanic material across the surrounding terrain. These deposits preserve a record of the mountain’s turbulent past.
One of the most intriguing features of Shivelyuch is its enormous caldera, a depression measuring approximately 5.6 miles (nine kilometers) across.
Within this depression, a lava dome has developed as magma reaches the surface. The dome stands out against the snow in the satellite image.
Unlike the fluid lava commonly associated with Hawaiian volcanoes, the thick lava that builds volcanic domes does not travel easily across the landscape.
Instead, it accumulates around the opening from which it emerges.
As more material reaches the surface, the dome can expand, develop fractures, and become increasingly unstable.
Sections of these domes sometimes collapse. Such events can unleash pyroclastic flows – rapidly moving mixtures of scorching gas, ash, and fragmented rock that sweep down a volcano’s slopes.
The process can dramatically alter the appearance of a mountain, sometimes within minutes.
Kamchatka’s extraordinary volcanic landscape owes its existence to the movement of enormous sections of Earth’s outer shell.
The peninsula sits along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a vast region of geological activity surrounding much of the Pacific Ocean.
Here, the Pacific tectonic plate descends beneath another plate in a process called subduction.
Water released from the descending plate promotes melting in the overlying mantle, generating magma that can eventually rise toward the surface.
Over millions of years, this process has created a remarkable concentration of volcanoes, along with hot springs, geysers, and other geothermal features.
Kamchatka provides scientists with an opportunity to observe some of the fundamental processes responsible for reshaping Earth’s surface.
The effects of volcanic activity at Shivelyuch can extend well beyond the peninsula.
Although volcanic ash resembles ordinary dust, it consists of tiny fragments of rock, minerals, and volcanic glass.
These abrasive particles can damage aircraft engines and other critical equipment.
High-altitude winds can carry ash clouds across international borders and oceans. In July 2026, ash from Shivelyuch reached Alaskan airspace after traveling across the Bering Sea, disrupting air travel.
Even between major explosions, previously deposited ash can become airborne again when strong winds sweep across the landscape.
This means that an ash plume does not necessarily indicate that a new explosive eruption has occurred.
Volcanic activity at Shivelyuch had persisted for several months when Landsat 9 acquired this image.
Monitoring a remote volcano surrounded by unpredictable weather presents considerable challenges.
Satellites offer scientists an invaluable perspective on places where direct observations are difficult.
In addition to capturing changes in the appearance of volcanic landscapes, instruments aboard some satellites can detect infrared radiation associated with unusually hot surfaces.
These measurements help researchers identify areas of elevated temperature that may be associated with freshly exposed lava or other volcanic activity.
By comparing observations collected over extended periods, scientists can also track the growth and destruction of lava domes, map volcanic deposits, and document changes to the surrounding environment.
Weather clouds can interfere with many of these observations, making clear views of active volcanic features particularly valuable.
Seen from hundreds of miles above Earth, Shivelyuch appears almost serene. Its snow-covered slopes emerge from the clouds, revealing a rugged summit seemingly isolated from the world below.
Yet the mountain’s appearance belies the geological activity taking place beneath its surface.
The dark lava dome visible in today’s image represents the latest chapter in a history of destruction and renewal spanning thousands of years.
Long after the surrounding clouds have dispersed, the forces responsible for building Shivelyuch will continue to transform the mountain.

item.page_text:
The Flights in the Air Right Now map from Tailodds displays two things: the live positions of aircraft flying over the United States and the wind conditions at cruising altitude.
There are plenty of maps showing the real-time positions of commercial aircraft, but this one puts that flight data to an ingenious additional use. What differentiates the Tailodds map from FlightRadar24 and FlightAware is that the wind conditions on this map don't come from a weather service but are inferred from the aircraft themselves.
The wind conditions on Flights in the Air Right Now are calculated by comparing the direction an aircraft is pointing (its heading) with the direction it is actually travelling (its ground track). Because aircraft have to compensate for wind, these two directions aren't necessarily the same. When flying across a crosswind, for example, a pilot will point the nose slightly into the wind to maintain the intended flight path. This is known as 'crabbing'.
By analysing the differences between the headings and ground tracks of multiple aircraft travelling in different directions, Tailodds can calculate the wind's direction and speed. The map's creator uses around 2,500 airliners flying at cruising altitude over a 30-minute period to calculate wind conditions across approximately 750 one-degree geographic areas. The results are refreshed every 30 minutes.
Remarkably, the calculations use no conventional weather data. Instead, they rely on publicly available ADS-B aircraft tracking data from adsb.fi, with magnetic headings converted to true north using the World Magnetic Model.
It is an ingenious way of turning commercial airliners into flying weather stations. And it isn't just a clever experiment: some meteorological services also use ADS-B and Mode-S aircraft tracking data to derive upper-level winds. The Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (KNMI), for example, has researched and implemented systems that turn routine aircraft surveillance messages into real-time upper-air wind observations for weather forecasting.

item.title: Middle East conflict: Smoke seen from space after attack on key Saudi Arabia oil hub - Nine
item.summary: Smoke seen from space after attack on huge Middle East oil hub ... satellite image shows a large smoke cloud billowing over Saudi Arabia's ...
item.page_text:
Satellite imagery showed a huge plume of black smoke rising from Saudi Arabia’s coastal Ras Tanura peninsula after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed to have attacked the kingdom’s biggest oil refinery.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the strikes “were accurate and direct” and caused a fire at the Ras Tanura facility, part of one of the world’s largest crude oil export terminals.
A satellite image shows a large smoke cloud billowing over Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery after Yemen’s Houthi military leadership said in a statement that they attacked the industrial facility. 2026 PLANET LABS PBC/Reuters via CNN
A shipping source told CNN overnight that oil loadings at the terminal were suspended after the attack. It’s unclear whether they have resumed.
The Houthis have targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia repeatedly in recent weeks – including an attack on the capital Riyadh’s financial district – as the fallout from the US-Iran war drags on.
Riyadh’s international airport was also hit several times last month, killing more than a dozen people.
On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition battling the Houthi rebels said it intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in the kingdom’s eastern province.
The interception resulted in falling debris, but no injuries were reported, the Coalition Forces spokesman Major General Turki Al-Malki said, citing an initial assessment.
Ras Tanura, which has been targeted previously during the conflict, has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day and is part of a broader coastal complex that housed the kingdom’s main export terminal before the US-Iran war began in late February.
CNN has approached Saudi state-owned oil giant Aramco for comment.
Separately on Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had attacked “operational capabilities” in the Houthi-controlled Hodeidah port and “destroyed a number of targets” in Saada and Amran governorates, as tit-for-tat strikes between the two sides escalate.
Houthi-affiliated al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi-led forces launched airstrikes on Hodeidah city, including an attack at the Hodeidah International Airport.
Smoke billows from the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Thursday after Houthi media reported a series of Saudi airstrikes against territories held by the Iran-backed group. AFP/Getty Images via CNN
The port at Hodeidah serves as a key supply route for the Houthis.
Several Saudi airstrikes were reported on Thursday, including on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, according to al-Masirah TV.
CNN has not been able to independently verify the attacks.
Fighting between the Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition reignited in July after years of relative calm brought about by a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire.
The Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower in Riyadh’s Financial district which the Saudi-led coalition said had been targeted by a “terrorist attack” on Tuesday. Saudi Press Agency via CNN
Clashes intensified in recent months after the militant group made an advance toward the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, threatening a new front in the Iran war.
In their Wednesday statement, the Houthis also claimed responsibility for a strike on the King Abdullah Economic City in Riyadh that Saudi authorities said wounded 11 people. It was the third such attack this month in the Saudi capital.
In response to the Riyadh attack, the Saudi-led coalition said the “deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian objects by the Houthi terrorist militia will be met with a firm response.”
An eyewitness in Riyadh told CNN the targeted building, the tallest in the Saudi capital, was the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s trillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF). The skyscraper was also struck earlier this month in a missile attack.

item.title: Brazil's Christ the Redeemer Appears To Float Above a Sea of Clouds, Leaving Viewers ...
item.summary: From Amaro's vantage point, cloud appears to pour down the mountainside. Baddini's aerial footage shows the monument above a blanket of cloud ...
item.page_text:
Brazil's Christ the Redeemer appeared to float above Rio de Janeiro on Saturday, 21 November, as clouds concealed much of Corcovado Mountain beneath it. Footage of the scene spread across social media, where users questioned whether the images were genuine or had been created using artificial intelligence (AI) .
The scene was recorded in the early hours, as a thick layer of cloud moved across the mountain. The statue remained visible while clouds appeared to spill down the slopes below it, creating the impression of a waterfall beneath its outstretched arms.
Brazilian filmmaker and photographer Márcio Amaro filmed the scene on his mobile phone from the Santa Teresa neighbourhood. Photographer Humberto Baddini also captured it using a drone, according to a report by NTN24 on 26 November.
The recordings show different views of the same weather event. From Amaro's vantage point, cloud appears to pour down the mountainside. Baddini's aerial footage shows the monument above a blanket of cloud, with much of the surrounding land obscured.
The Times of India reported on 25 November that social media users had questioned whether the images were real . The landmark's appearance, seemingly separated from the ground, also prompted speculation about possible AI involvement.
Amaro said his recording was genuine and had not been generated using AI , according to Euronews. He also said he had never seen Corcovado look quite like this before.
His statement concerned his own recording, rather than every version of the imagery shared online. The footage and reports cited do not establish whether other images circulating online were altered or generated .
Rio's coastal geography helps explain the scene. Corcovado rises to about 710 metres above sea level and can intercept moist winds arriving from the Atlantic Ocean.
When wind pushes moist air uphill, the air encounters lower atmospheric pressure, expands and cools. If it cools enough, water vapour condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds. Meteorologists call the upward movement of air caused by terrain orographic lift.
The World Meteorological Organization explains that mountains can affect cloud formation at different elevations. Depending on the atmospheric conditions, clouds may form below a summit, around it or higher above it.
Wind can also carry cloud over a ridge and down a slope, producing what looks like a waterfall. As air descends, it generally warms, which can cause cloud droplets to evaporate and the cloud to dissipate.
The height and movement of the cloud layer determine whether the statue and the land below it remain visible. In this footage, much of Corcovado was hidden, making it difficult to distinguish the ground beneath the monument, particularly from a distance.
Euronews reported that similar scenes were photographed in August 2026. Those images showed fog settled in the valleys, rather than clouds cascading down the hillside.
Completed in 1931, Christ the Redeemer stands within Tijuca National Park. New7Wonders gives the concrete and soapstone figure's height as 30 metres, excluding its eight-metre pedestal, and its arm span as 28 metres.
The monument overlooks Rio de Janeiro and Guanabara Bay and is recognised as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. On 21 November, cloud obscured much of the landscape around it, leaving the statue visible above the slopes.
